title: Galileo, honestly (1633)
hookLine: the Church condemned Galileo; in 1992 John Paul II acknowledged the error

cards: A tube of glass and wood, pointed at the night sky over Italy. Through it, the moon has mountains. Jupiter has small lights circling it.
The man at the eyepiece writes it all up in a short book with a Latin title, the Starry Messenger. He is a Catholic, a professor, and very sure of himself.
What he's seeing points to an idea that the earth moves around the sun, and some in the Church will call that idea against the Scriptures. His name is Galileo.

teach.b: First, the argument. Galileo's critics pointed to passages like the one where Joshua commands the sun to stand still. If the sun stands still, they said, it must normally move.

teach.h: HOW TO GO TO HEAVEN, NOT HOW IT GOES.
teach.b: Galileo answered in a long letter, quoting a churchman of his day: the Holy Spirit means to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go.
Scripture, he argued, speaks the way ordinary people speak about sunrise. Second, the condemnation. The Holy Office in Rome ruled against the idea, and later put Galileo on trial.
He was made to kneel and formally renounce the view that the earth moves.
He spent the rest of his life confined to his house near Florence, and kept working. He was not burned, and he remained a Catholic. Third, the legend.
People say that as he rose from his knees he muttered, and yet it moves.

teach.h: AND YET IT MOVES: A LATER STORY.
teach.b: It's a good line, but it isn't in the trial records; it's a story told later. Fourth, the admission. Centuries later, Pope John Paul the Second asked for the case to be studied again.
Speaking to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, he acknowledged that the theologians who condemned Galileo had erred, and called the affair a tragic mutual misunderstanding.
A pope had said, in public, that the condemnation was a mistake. Some Catholics pair this with the Psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God."
For those who pray it, the Psalm and the telescope look at the same sky.

how: The Vatican keeps an observatory and a Pontifical Academy of Sciences, and Catholic teaching holds that faith and reason cannot truly contradict each other.

games.q: you're Galileo. critics say the Bible shows the sun moves, because Joshua told it to stand still. what do you answer?
o: the Bible is wrong, so ignore it.
Scripture teaches how one goes to heaven, not how the heavens go.
you're right; I'll stop looking through the telescope.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you got wrong and haven't quite owned: a judgment about someone, an argument you shouldn't have won, something you insisted on that turned out false.
Let it be what it was, then picture saying it plainly to the person it touched: I was wrong about that. If you pray, bring it to God first; if you don't, simply practice the words.

wordCard.voice: Galileo. The Catholic astronomer whose telescope findings backed a moving earth, who was condemned in Rome, and whose case a pope later called an error.

orig.note: Latin: the Starry Messenger, the title of Galileo's short book about what his telescope showed.

carryVoice: Your line: the error, admitted. It took centuries, and it still counted. See you tomorrow.
